subModules.grammarFocus: Second Conditional (If + Past Simple, would + base verb)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Life choices, hypothetical situations, and ambitions

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will explore short stories and blog posts about people imagining different lives. You will learn how to use the second conditional to talk about imaginary situations and unreal dreams in the present or future.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Second conditional sentences using If plus past simple, followed by would and the base form of the verb.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words related to life choices, ambitions, and hypothetical situations like lottery, career, and adventure.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific hypothetical outcomes and skimming paragraphs to understand main life goals.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of short A2 texts about imaginary scenarios.
Locate specific details such as hypothetical results and personal choices.
Recognize and practice second conditional grammar patterns in context.

contextWarmup.prompt: What would you do if you found a bag full of money on the street?
options: I would take it to the police station.
I would buy a new video game.
I would hide it in my room.
contextWarmup.explanation: Taking found money to the police station is the responsible and honest choice in this imaginary situation.

rules: Formula: If plus subject plus past simple, subject plus would plus base verb. Example: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
Use 'were' for all subjects (I, he, she, it, we, you, they) in formal second conditional sentences. Example: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
The if clause and main clause can switch places. If the if clause comes first, use a comma. Example: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Using will instead of would in the result clause
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up first and second conditionals. Second conditionals talk about unreal or imaginary situations, so you must use would, not will.
commonTrap.wrong: If I had a million dollars, I will buy a car.
commonTrap.correct: If I had a million dollars, I would buy a car.

paragraphs: Every year, a local teen magazine asks students about their biggest dreams and imaginary scenarios. Maya, a fifteen-year-old student from London, shared her thoughts. She said that if she won the lottery, she would buy a big house near the beach. She also mentioned that if she had a million dollars, she would donate half of it to local animal shelters.

Another student, Leo, has different ambitions. Leo loves languages and travel. He explained that if he were fluent in Spanish and French, he would travel across South America and Europe without a guide. Furthermore, Leo believes that if he had the opportunity to study abroad next year, he would take it immediately to build a better career for his future.

questions.question: Choose the correct second conditional sentence structure.
options: If I had money, I would buy a car.
If I have money, I will buy a car.
If I had money, I will buy a car.
questions.answer: If I had money, I would buy a car.
questions.explanation: Second conditional uses past simple in the if clause and would plus base verb in the result clause.

questions.question: Why do we use 'were' instead of 'was' in formal second conditional sentences like 'If I were rich'?
options: It is a rule for all subjects in hypothetical situations.
It is only used for plural nouns.
It is a mistake in grammar.
questions.answer: It is a rule for all subjects in hypothetical situations.
questions.explanation: In formal second conditional sentences, 'were' is used for all subjects to express unreal situations.

questions.question: What does the word 'career' mean in Indonesian?
questions.explanation: The Indonesian meaning for 'career' is karier or jalur profesi.

questions.question: If someone wants to invest in property, what are they doing?

questions.answer: Putting money into buildings or land to make a profit
questions.explanation: To invest means to put money into something like property to gain financial returns.

questions.question: When skimming a text about imaginary scenarios, what should you look for?

The exact dates of past events
questions.answer: General ideas about what people would do in unreal situations
questions.explanation: Skimming helps you quickly grasp the main themes and hypothetical outcomes of the text.

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation between two friends discussing imaginary situations and future wishes using second conditional structures. Pay attention to how speakers use past verb forms to talk about unreal present or future possibilities, and notice how words blend together in fast spoken English.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about imaginary situations.
Identify details about conditional preferences and wishes.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during conditional sentences.

keyPhrases.note: Used to ask about someone's reaction in an imaginary situation.
Introduces an unreal present or future condition.
Common phrase used to give advice based on imagination.
Meaning to begin something again from the beginning.

connectedSpeech.note: The sounds /d/ and /y/ blend together to make a /dʒ/ sound.
The pronoun 'I' and auxiliary 'had' link smoothly, often dropping the /h/ sound.
Spoken with a smooth liaison between conditional 'if' and subject 'I'.
The word 'about' links to 'you', changing the /t/ sound into a soft blend.

content.summary: Practical guide on sentence structure and paragraph building for imaginary scenarios using the second conditional in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Second Conditional Basic Formula
blueprintItems.formula: If + Subject + Past Simple, Subject + would + Verb (base form)
blueprintItems.example: If I had more money, I would buy a fast car.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Using 'Were' for All Subjects
blueprintItems.formula: If + Subject (I / he / she / it / we / you / they) + were + complement, Subject + would + Verb
blueprintItems.example: If she were here, she would help us with our homework.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Changing Clause Order
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + would + Verb + if + Subject + Past Simple (no comma)
blueprintItems.example: I would travel around the world if I won the lottery.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always put a comma after the 'if' clause when it comes first in a sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If I lived near the beach I would swim every day.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If I lived near the beach, I would swim every day.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the conditional clause from the main result clause.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the base form of the verb after 'would', not an -ing form or past tense.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If I had a camera, I would taking photos.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If I had a camera, I would take photos.
mechanicsRules.why: Modal verbs like 'would' are always followed by the base infinitive verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'were' instead of 'was' for all subjects in formal conditional imaginary statements.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If I was a bird, I would fly high in the sky.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If I were a bird, I would fly high in the sky.
mechanicsRules.why: In second conditional grammar, 'were' is standard for unreal present states with all pronouns.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the second conditional structure:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I don't have a bicycle, so I walk to school.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'If I had a bicycle...'
targetAnswers: If I had a bicycle, I would ride to school.
If I had a bicycle, I would not walk to school.
If I had a bicycle, I would ride it to school.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Change present simple 'don't have' to past simple 'had', and use 'would' with the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two clauses into a correct second conditional sentence starting with the 'if' clause:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I see a ghost / I run away
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember the comma after the if clause.
targetAnswers: If I saw a ghost, I would run away.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past simple 'saw' in the if clause, add a comma, and use 'would run' in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the grammatical error in this second conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: if i was rich i will buy a big house
practicumQuestions.hint: Check capitalization, 'were' instead of 'was', and 'would' instead of 'will'.
targetAnswers: If I were rich, I would buy a big house.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Capitalize 'If', use 'were' for the conditional state, add a comma, and use 'would buy' instead of 'will buy'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this positive second conditional sentence into a negative result sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If it rained, we would go outside.
targetAnswers: If it rained, we wouldn't go outside.
If it rained, we would not go outside.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Make the result clause negative by using 'wouldn't' or 'would not' before the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the second conditional sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If she (know) the answer, she would tell us.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the past simple form of 'know'.
targetAnswers: If she knew the answer, she would tell us.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The past simple form of 'know' is 'knew'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence placing the main clause first (no comma):
practicumQuestions.promptText: If I lived in Paris, I would speak French every day.
practicumQuestions.hint: Put 'I would speak French every day' at the beginning.
targetAnswers: I would speak French every day if I lived in Paris.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When the main clause comes first, do not use a comma before 'if'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the punctuation and verb form in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: What you would do if you find a wallet on the street
practicumQuestions.hint: Add auxiliary verb 'would' correctly in a question and use past simple 'found'.
targetAnswers: What would you do if you found a wallet on the street?
practicumQuestions.explanation: In second conditional questions, use 'What would + subject + verb' and past simple 'found' in the if clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with 'was' or 'were' according to formal second conditional grammar:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If I _____ a famous singer, I would give free concerts.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'were' for all subjects in formal conditional sentences.
targetAnswers: If I were a famous singer, I would give free concerts.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In formal second conditional sentences, 'were' is used for all persons including I, he, she, and it.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Create a second conditional sentence from the prompt:
practicumQuestions.promptText: have a magic wand / turn the desert into a forest
practicumQuestions.hint: If I had a magic wand, I would turn the desert into a forest.
targetAnswers: If I had a magic wand, I would turn the desert into a forest.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'had' in the if clause and 'would turn' in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the error in this second conditional sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: If he worked harder, he will pass the exam.
targetAnswers: If he worked harder, he would pass the exam.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Second conditional requires 'would' + base verb in the result clause, not 'will'.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Imaginary Scenarios and Dreams

content.summary: This module guides you through speaking about imaginary situations and future dreams using the second conditional. You will learn how to link words smoothly, use contractions like I would to I would or I'd, and control sentence stress to sound natural.
content.audioGuidance: Keep your voice steady and stress the main action verbs and nouns in both clauses. Use a slight pause between the if clause and the main clause to make your meaning clear to listeners.

pillars.name: Conditional Rhythm
pillars.explanation: Pronounce the past simple verb clearly in the if clause, then use a clear contraction for would in the main clause.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.explanation: Highlight words like lottery, million, island, and fluent so listeners immediately understand the hypothetical nature of your statement.

pillars.name: Intonation Contours
pillars.target: Rising tone for conditions and falling tone for outcomes
pillars.explanation: Raise your pitch slightly at the end of the if clause, and let your voice drop at the end of the main clause.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how stress shifts from the first syllable in lottery to the second syllable in million.
Notice that island places stress on the first syllable, while adventure places stress on the second syllable.
Both adjectives have primary stress on their first syllable.
Notice that invest stresses the second syllable, while volunteer places primary stress on the final syllable.

practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence using correct vocabulary and clear vowel sounds.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If I had the opportunity, I would invest my money wisely.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ hæd ði ˌɒp.əˈtʃuː.nə.ti, aɪ wʊd ɪnˈvest maɪ ˈmʌn.i ˈwaɪz.li/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Focus on accurate pronunciation of opportunity and invest.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the second conditional sentence with accurate grammar structure.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence focusing on the past simple and would auxiliary verb.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If I were rich, I would buy a private island.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ wɜːr rɪtʃ, aɪ wʊd baɪ ə ˈpraɪ.vət ˈaɪ.lənd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure you use were with I and emphasize the modal verb would.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice correct syllable stress on multi-syllable words.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read the sentence and stress the word confident correctly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If I were more confident, I would speak in public easily.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ wɜːr mɔːr ˈkɒn.fɪ.dənt, aɪ wʊd spiːk ɪn ˈpʌb.lɪk ˈiː.zɪ.li/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place primary stress on the first syllable of confident.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice rising intonation in the if clause and falling intonation in the main clause.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read the sentence using a rising pitch on the condition and falling pitch on the result.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If I won the lottery, I would travel around the world.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ wʌn ðə ˈlɒt.ər.i, aɪ wʊd ˈtræv.əl əˈraʊnd ðə wɜːld/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Raise your voice slightly at the end of lottery and lower it at the end of world.
